articles.title: ANTHBOT N8 : le robot tondeuse 4-en-1 qui tond, mulche, collecte et balaie tout seul
articles.text:
ANTHBOT N8 : le robot tondeuse 4-en-1 qui tond, mulche, collecte et balaie tout seul
ANTHBOT lance le N8, présenté comme un robot tondeuse 4 en 1 capable de tondre, mulcher, collecter les résidus et balayer les feuilles mortes sans aucun besoin d’intervention humaine. Autant dire que l’outil entend transformer la tonte robobtisée, surtout que celle-ci était jusqu’ici limitée à couper l’herbe en laissant le reste du travail au propriétaire. Ici, ce dernier peut se la couler douce pendant le robot s’occupe de tout. Ce nouveau modèle sera commercialisé le 10 septembre prochain, pour 1 599€.
Nous avons une chose simple à vous dire à propos du marché des robots tondeuses : il s’est jusqu’ici un peu trop reposé sur ses lauriers, en se concentrant principalement sur l’automatisation de la coupe elle-même, laissant de côté tout ce qui vient après. Et ce qui vient après, ce n’est pas une mince affaire non plus : on parle des résidus de tonte éparpillés sur la pelouse, de la pousse dense de l'été qui dépasse les capacités du système de coupe, ou même des feuilles mortes de l'automne qui s'accumulent sans que le robot ne puisse les prendre en charge.
Un système de coupe modulaire pour ne plus rien ramasser à la main
Le N8 répond précisément à ces trois angles morts avec un système de coupe modulaire, à adapter selon la saison ou l'état du jardin. Le Cyclone Sweeping System utilise le flux d'air généré par la rotation des lames pour aspirer jusqu'à 99 % des résidus de tonte ou des feuilles mortes dans un bac de 23 litres, pour une pelouse visiblement propre après chaque passage, sans besoin que l’on ramasse les résidus par nous-même. Le Particle Mulching System, lui, mise sur un système à 6 lames pour broyer finement l'herbe coupée et la disperser uniformément, réduisant de fait les amas disgracieux tout en recyclant les nutriments dans le sol plutôt que de les évacuer.
Une fois le bac plein, c’est là que la magie opère, avec la fonction Hands-Free Auto Dumping qui prend directement le relais : par cette méthode, le robot vide automatiquement son contenu dans une zone désignée depuis l'application, sans qu'il soit nécessaire d'aller vider soi-même le bac de collecte à chaque cycle de tonte. Et c’est précisément cette tâche qui reste habituellement manuelle sur la majorité des robots collecteurs actuels du marché.
Une navigation sans fil précise au centimètre
Le N8 illustre bien l'argument d’absence de câble porté par la marque : ici, vous n’aurez aucun câble périphérique à enterrer avant la première utilisation, contrairement aux modèles de première génération encore bien répandus sur le marché. La navigation combine quant à elle un positionnement Full-Band RTK et une double vision par IA, pour une précision annoncée au centimètre près et une stabilité de navigation aussi bien sur une pelouse dégagée que dans une allée ombragée ou sous un abri de jardin, des zones où les robots reposant sur une seule technologie de positionnement perdent généralement en fiabilité. Pour les foyers qui préfèrent se passer d'une borne RTK physique, le robot reste compatible avec le NetRTK via une connexion 4G suffisamment stable.
Taillé pour les grands jardins
Vous nous permettrez bien un petit temps alloué aux chiffres, pour tous les amateurs de fiche technique : le N8 promet une surface de tonte recommandée allant jusqu'à 1 500 m², avec une efficacité de coupe maximale de 135 m²/h. De son côté, la batterie lithium-ion de 9,2 Ah (198 Wh) se recharge en 80 minutes, et le robot grimpe des pentes jusqu'à 45 % (24°) sans difficulté. Au niveau du confort d'usage, jusqu'à 30 zones distinctes peuvent être cartographiées et reliées entre elles par des ponts virtuels, la hauteur de coupe se règle directement depuis l'application, et un capteur de pluie intégré adapte automatiquement le calendrier de tonte selon la météo. Certifié IPX6, le N8 reste également discret, avec un niveau sonore de 58 dB maximum en tonte et mulching, et 68 dB lors des phases de collecte et de balayage.
Disponibilité
Le ANTHBOT N8 sera disponible à partir du 10 septembre 2026, au prix de 1 599 €. En France, vous pourrez retrouver l’appareil à la fois sur le site officiel de la firme, mais aussi chez des revendeurs français comme Boulanger.
Retrouvez plus d'informations sur eu.anthbot.com

articles.title: Mandiant Founder Kevin Mandia Joins Amazon Board
articles.text:
Amazon has appointed cybersecurity veteran Kevin Mandia to its board of directors, strengthening the technology giant’s security expertise at the board level.
Mandia was elected to the board on September 8 and brings more than 30 years of experience responding to cyber threats across the public and private sectors, Amazon announced.
He is the founder and CEO of cybersecurity firm Armadin and a co-founder and general partner at cybersecurity-focused venture capital firm Ballistic Ventures.
Mandia is best known as the founder and former CEO of incident response and threat intelligence company Mandiant. The company was acquired by FireEye in late 2013, but regained its name in 2021 after FireEye sold its products business. Google subsequently acquired Mandiant in 2022 and integrated the company into Google Cloud.
Before entering the private sector, Mandia served as a computer security officer at the Pentagon and as a special agent in the Air Force Office of Special Investigations. He has also served on the National Security Telecommunications Advisory Committee and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s Cybersecurity Advisory Committee.
Amazon said Mandia’s experience defending large organizations and investing in emerging security companies will help inform its board as cybersecurity risks evolve alongside advances in artificial intelligence.
“His election reflects our commitment to having appropriate experience and perspectives at all levels of the company, including our Board of Directors,” Amazon said.
Related: Former NSA Director Paul Nakasone Launches National Security Advisory Firm

articles.title: Avec l'iPhone Duo sans Face ID, Apple fait un retour dans le temps
articles.text:
Lors d’une keynote historique, Apple a enfin levé le voile sur son tout premier iPhone pliant, l’iPhone Duo. Comme le voulaient les rumeurs, l’iPhone le plus cher de l’histoire de la marque fait l’impasse sur une technologie phare : Face ID.
Inaugurée il y a bientôt dix ans au moment de la sortie de l’iPhone X, la reconnaissance faciale d’Apple s’est imposée comme l’une des fonctions phares des téléphones estampillés Apple. D’abord réservé aux modèles les plus premium, Face ID s’est progressivement imposé sur tous les iPhone, y compris sur les versions plus abordables. La reconnaissance a graduellement remplacé Touch ID, le capteur d’empreintes digitales apparu avec les iPhone 5S en 2023.
À lire aussi : iPhone Duo – les 5 règles qu’Apple a mises à la poubelle avec son smartphone pliant
Retour vers le passé pour l’iPhone du futur
Avec son tout premier iPhone pliable, Apple opère un retour arrière inattendu. L’iPhone Duo embarque en effet un lecteur d’empreintes digitales, situé sur la tranche dans le bouton d’alimentation. On retrouve la même logique sur les iPad Air. Cette approche permet de déverrouiller l’appareil de la même façon, quel que soit l’état du téléphone, à savoir ouvert ou fermé. Apple précise que « les utilisateurs peuvent également déverrouiller l’iPhone Duo avec leur Apple Watch », comme c’est le cas sur les MacBooks.
Le groupe californien n’a probablement pas eu assez de place pour glisser tous les capteurs TrueDepth, indispensables au fonctionnement de Face ID, dans la structure sans l’épaissir. En faisant l’impasse sur ces capteurs, Apple parvient à proposer un iPhone pliable particulièrement fin. Il ne mesure en effet que 4,5 mm d’épaisseur, ce qui en fait officiellement l’iPhone le plus fin jamais conçu par Apple. Il est même plus fin que l’iPhone Air, dont c’est l’un des principaux arguments de vente.
À lire aussi : Apple explique comment l’iPhone Duo échappe à l’un des plus gros défauts des smartphones pliants
Aussi futuriste soit l’iPhone Duo, le smartphone signe un retour vers le passé, à l’époque où il fallait poser son doigt sur un capteur pour déverrouiller son iPhone. C’est un vrai changement d’habitude pour les utilisateurs habitués depuis des années à Face ID.

articles.title: Las células de tu cuerpo ‘hablan’ entre sí y una IA logró traducir su idioma
articles.text:
Las células del cuerpo humano se comunican todo el tiempo entre sí. Lo hacen con señales químicas que funcionan como mensajes: le avisan a cada célula en qué etapa del desarrollo está y qué debe convertirse, ya sea una neurona, una célula del corazón o parte de un pulmón. Ahora, gracias a la inteligencia artificial, esa conversación puede entenderse.
Un equipo del Instituto Whitehead, liderado por Pulin Li y Nicholas Hutchins, creó un sistema capaz de leer esos mensajes celulares. El hallazgo podría cambiar la forma en que se estudian enfermedades complejas como el asma o la fibrosis pulmonar.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo es la IA que traduce el idioma de las celulas
El sistema se llama IRIS y funciona como un programa entrenado para reconocer patrones dentro de la actividad genética de las células. Li lo compara con algo mucho más cotidiano: los asistentes de voz.
“Piensa en los sistemas de reconocimiento de voz como Siri, que se entrenan principalmente en inglés, pero que luego utilizan ese entrenamiento para reconocer otros idiomas”, explicó la investigadora, que además es profesora de biología en el Instituto Tecnológico de Massachusetts (MIT).
PUBLICIDAD
Es decir, así como Siri puede aplicar lo aprendido en un idioma para entender otro, IRIS aprende a reconocer un tipo de señal en un grupo de células y luego logra identificar esa misma señal en células completamente distintas. A este truco se lo llama aprendizaje por transferencia.
IRIS es un sistema de inteligencia artificial que aprende a reconocer las señales químicas que reciben las células y, con esa información, predice en qué tejido se convertirán. Funciona de forma parecida a un traductor: identifica un patrón en el “idioma” celular y anticipa la decisión que tomará esa célula, incluso en tejidos que nunca vio antes.
PUBLICIDAD
Para enseñarle ese idioma, los investigadores trabajaron con células madre de ratón y de humano. Sobre ellas, encendieron y apagaron de forma controlada seis señales químicas distintas que el cuerpo usa naturalmente para dirigir el desarrollo embrionario.
Combinaron esas señales de miles de formas diferentes y observaron, con tecnología de análisis genético, cómo reaccionaba cada célula en cada caso. Con todos esos datos armaron algo similar a un mapa: si a una célula le llega tal combinación de señales, el mapa indica hacia qué destino se dirige.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo comprobaron que la inteligencia artificial funcionaba
El primer examen se hizo con embriones de ratón, en el momento en que sus células empiezan a transformarse en los tejidos principales del cuerpo. IRIS logró anticipar con precisión qué señales llevarían a la formación del corazón, los intestinos, los músculos y la médula espinal.
Después llegó una prueba más exigente: la del proceso mediante el cual el cuerpo del embrión se organiza en segmentos, algo así como ordenar piezas en fila según señales que llegan desde dos direcciones opuestas. IRIS consiguió ordenar correctamente esas señales sin haber sido entrenado específicamente para esa tarea.
PUBLICIDAD
También lo pusieron a prueba con células nerviosas que nunca había visto antes durante su entrenamiento. Aun así, sus predicciones coincidieron con lo que ya se sabía sobre cómo se forma el sistema nervioso en las primeras etapas.
Por qué este descubrimiento puede ser útil para la medicina
Más allá de explicar cómo se forman los tejidos de manera natural, IRIS mostró que también puede servir para mejorar procesos de laboratorio. Los investigadores lo usaron para perfeccionar la manera en que se cultivan, a partir de células madre, los tejidos que sostienen los pulmones.
PUBLICIDAD
El método que se usaba hasta ahora activaba una de las señales, llamada WNT, en una etapa tardía del proceso. Pero IRIS predijo algo distinto: que esa señal era importante mucho antes, en el momento en el que la célula recién empieza a definirse como parte del sistema respiratorio.
Con ese dato, los científicos decidieron activar la señal antes y durante más tiempo. El resultado fue contundente: aumentó de forma notable la presencia de una proteína clave para formar tejido pulmonar, y una intensidad media de la señal resultó ser la más adecuada para lograr un tejido lo más parecido posible al real.
PUBLICIDAD
El experimento funcionó de igual manera al repetirlo con distintos tipos de células madre, lo que refuerza la idea de que el nuevo método se acerca más a lo que ocurre de forma natural dentro del cuerpo.
Los propios investigadores aclaran que ajustar una sola señal no alcanza todavía para fabricar en laboratorio un tejido pulmonar idéntico al que produce el organismo. Sin embargo, creen que si combinan esta herramienta con mapas más completos sobre cómo se desarrolla el pulmón, podrían acercarse cada vez más a ese objetivo.

articles.title: “Valuable warning shots”: How Anthropic now views Claude’s cyber incidents
articles.text:
“Valuable warning shots”: How Anthropic now views Claude’s cyber incidents
This week, Anthropic acknowledged that the three cyber incidents it disclosed this summer weren’t just the result of a misconfigured test environment. It turns out that Claude’s own behavior was part of the problem.
Recall in July when the AI company released a report on three cases where Claude models reached the open internet from misconfigured test environments and compromised real third-party systems — a telling example of the limits of AI safety tests and why AI evaluation infrastructure needs production-grade security.
Upon deeper review, Anthropic now says that explanation was incomplete. Beyond the operational failure, the models themselves displayed two recurring alignment failures: biased reasoning and recklessness. And, actually, there was a fourth incident that the AI company only found out about after further investigation.
It’s awkward timing, given one of Anthropic’s pretraining researchers, Jacob Coxon, resigned this week due to concerns about superintelligence that “could kill us all,” taking to X to write:
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately.”
The incidents definitely don’t prove this kind of risk, but they do illuminate how models can behave unexpectedly — and how existing evaluations can fail to catch it.
The problem was more than an operational failure
This summer, when Anthropic shared its initial findings, it said the three cyber incidents were “closer to a harness and operational failure than a model alignment failure,” with Claude seeming to believe it was operating in a simulation without internet access.
But a closer look at the transcripts revealed that the problem was not simply the model reaching the internet by mistake; Claude also showed signs of misaligned reasoning.
“When we made targeted modifications to the transcript to make it clearer that the model was not in a simulation, Claude Mythos 5 still took offensive actions, despite acknowledging a greater possibility of real-world harm.”
After widening the initial search to about 481 million transcripts, including those from the company’s Frontier Red Team, as well as non-cyber evaluations, reinforcement learning (RL) environments, subagent logs, and others, Anthropic conducted two scans.
First, it scanned these transcripts for signs of internet access, whittling down the pool to 9.2 million flagged for escalation. It then used Claude to review this smaller batch, re-identify the known incidents, and look for others of similar or worse severity.
What did it find? It found more than an operational failure. Anthropic says its investigation identified “two recurring alignment issues, present at varying levels of severity across the incidents.”
It names these issues as biased reasoning, where Claude disregarded or misinterpreted evidence that was, in fact, on the internet, and recklessness, where Claude was willing to take harmful actions to pursue a task.
Anthropic was already concerned that Claude Mythos 5 uploaded a malicious package to PyPI, but the model repeatedly said it believed it was operating in a simulation. Anthropic now says the simulation explanation does not fully account for the model’s behavior and that its reasoning appears to have been biased.
“When we made targeted modifications to the transcript to make it clearer that the model was not in a simulation, Claude Mythos 5 still took offensive actions, despite acknowledging a greater possibility of real-world harm.”
And there was a fourth incident Anthropic missed the first time
Anthropic’s new alignment assessment also contains another less than reassuring revelation: It missed one of the four incidents the first time around.
As the AI company explains, its first review relied on an agentic search due to “the volume of transcripts and [its] desire to disclose incidents quickly.” But that scan missed a set of transcripts that had also had internet access.
How did the cat get let out of the bag? It happened in August when Anthropic was assembling transcripts to share with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research). This research nonprofit measures whether and when AI systems might threaten catastrophic harm to society. The fourth incident dates from January 2026 and involves an early version of Claude Opus 4.6.
Discovering the fourth incident pushed Anthropic to broaden its search to the roughly 481 million transcripts described above, giving it more information to analyze and ultimately surfacing new insights into Claude’s “biased reasoning” and “recklessness.”
While this broader search didn’t turn up any more incidents of what Anthropic describes as “similar or worse severity,” the investigation isn’t over. Per the AI company, it’s signed an agreement with METR, granting the organization wide-ranging access to transcripts and Anthropic employees for eight weeks to investigate the incidents independently. The agreement can be extended if both parties agree.
Anthropic reproduced the failure to try to understand if newer models would do the same
Beyond reviewing the original incidents, Anthropic is taking other steps to try to understand how things went pear-shaped in the first place. It put Claude Opus 5 and Claude Mythos 5.1 in a simulated replication of the Mythos 5 scenario — the one where the model uploaded a malicious package to PyPI. Anthropic reports:
“Both take harmful actions substantially less often than Claude Mythos 5 did, but they still engage in the same behaviors at concerning rates.”
It notes that both models only took harmful actions after stating that they were, indeed, acting in a simulated environment. Anthropic also says that Mythos 5 appears to be “an outlier in terms of poor performance” on evaluations for biased reasoning, recklessness, and willingness to probe boundaries.
“Both take harmful actions substantially less often than Claude Mythos 5 did, but they still engage in the same behaviors at concerning rates.”
Still, it’s not such a clear indication of how the newer models would behave in the real world. As the AI company adds, “because the reproduction is, in fact, a simulation, we are cautious about how far these results generalize to the real world.”
Additionally, Anthropic looked back into its training to search for a root cause of Claude Mythos 5’s biased reasoning, but came up short. While it didn’t identify a single root cause, the company says biased reasoning decreased across its production models over time, potentially due to updated RL and alignment training.
Anthropic admits it still has work to do. Since its pre-release auditing didn’t catch misalignment of this severity, it’s since added evaluations to specifically target these behaviors, though reliably doing so is still a challenge.
Anthropic admits the failures were serious, but says they’re “narrow”
While Anthropic clearly calls out the four cyber incidents as “valuable warning shots,” it also points out that their scope was limited:
“While Claude’s actions were misaligned, they remained within a narrow scope,” the AI company says, pointing to the fact that all incidents included a single Claude instance and the model never attempted to coordinate with other agents or conceal evidence of its actions.
It says these behaviors playing out in ordinary use are “unlikely” and that, if they did, the safeguards shipped with production models would add more defenses that didn’t exist in these evaluations.
But following Coxon’s remarks about the risks of superintelligence, and Anthropic’s own alignment science lead, Evan Hubinger, responding that Anthropic “really do[es] earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” seeing Claude go off the rails isn’t comforting.

articles.title: iPhone Duo : sept ans après le Galaxy Fold, Apple entre dans une niche qui n'a jamais vraiment marché
articles.text:
Je vais commencer par une chose que personne n’aime dire lors des annonces de smartphones : le smartphone pliable n’a jamais marché. Pas vraiment.
Samsung y a mis sept ans, huit générations de Fold, des milliards en marketing et des remises qui feraient rougir un concessionnaire automobile. Huawei, Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Motorola ont suivi. Et en 2025, tout ce monde a vendu entre 18 et 21 millions de pliants selon le cabinet qu’on lit, sur un marché de 1,2 milliard de téléphones. Moins de 2 %. Au premier semestre 2026, Omdia mesure même un recul de 21,6 % sur un an. IDC est encore plus direct : sans Apple, la catégorie aurait fini l’année en baisse à deux chiffres. Sept ans, et on parle toujours d’une niche. Portée pour l’essentiel par la Chine, où Huawei fait la moitié des volumes.
    Pour aller plus loin
            Quels sont les meilleurs smartphones pliables en 2026 ? Samsung Galaxy Z, Honor Magic V, Motorola Razr… le comparatif
            
Ce n’est pas une question de qualité. Le Galaxy Z Fold 8 est un très bon téléphone, le Xiaomi 18 Fold certainement aussi, et j’ai eu dans les mains des Oppo Find N6 dont le format m’a fait envie pendant des semaines. Sans oublier les différentes générations de Pixel Fold Pro.
Le problème est ailleurs. Un pliant coûte le double d’un smartphone premium, pèse davantage, se protège moins bien, et propose surtout un grand écran à un moment où le reste de l’industrie explique que l’écran est en train de disparaître. Difficile de vendre un objet plus encombrant à des gens à qui on promet un futur sans objet. Les premières prises en main du Duo le confirment d’ailleurs à leur manière : le compliment le plus fréquent porte sur l’écran, la critique la plus lourde sur le poids.
Pour aller plus loin sur l’iPhone Duo
Ce qu’Apple change, et ce qu’elle ne peut pas changer
Apple arrive pourtant avec exactement ce qui manquait. Un milliard et demi d’iPhone actifs, un App Store qui impose une date aux développeurs, un système d’exploitation redessiné pour un seul appareil, et des Apple Store pour réparer une charnière à cent pièces dont une bonne partie des idées existait déjà chez Samsung et Xiaomi.
Les analystes ont fait le calcul avant même la keynote : IDC prévoit 17 millions de Duo en 2027, soit 40 % d’un marché que le seul iPhone ferait passer de 21 à 27 millions d’unités. Counterpoint est plus prudent, à 25 % dès cette année. Dans les deux cas, Apple ne rejoint pas le marché du pliant, elle en devient le marché, et Samsung passerait de 40 à 32 % de part sans vendre un téléphone de moins.
Protégez votre vie numérique et vos appareils contre les virus, arnaques, ransomwares et menaces en ligne avec Bitdefender, primé pour sa protection et compatible avec Windows, Mac, Android et iOS.
    Pour aller plus loin
            iPhone Duo : Apple présente son premier pliant, sept ans après le Galaxy Fold
            
Mais 27 millions d’unités, sur un marché qui va perdre 16,7 % de volume cette année et tomber sous les 1,1 milliard, c’est toujours 2,5 %. Le précédent que tout le monde cite, celui de l’iPad qui a fait exister la tablette en un trimestre, avait un ingrédient qui manque ici, le prix.
L’iPad de 2010 coûtait 499 euros. Le Duo coûte 2 339 euros, et IDC note que le marché entier se rétrécit parce que la mémoire est devenue trop chère.
Apple va rendre le pliant désirable, visible, normal dans une rame de métro. Elle ne va pas le rendre accessible, et sans accessibilité, une catégorie reste un objet de statut. Ce n’est pas rien, le Pro Max en est un aussi, mais ce n’est pas une révolution d’usage. Entre un 18 Pro et un Duo, la plupart des acheteurs choisiront d’ailleurs encore le premier, pour 860 euros de moins et un vrai téléobjectif.
    Pour aller plus loin
            iPhone 18 Pro ou iPhone Duo : le comparatif des compromis
            
Le parallèle qui revient depuis mardi soir, c’est le Vision Pro. Une catégorie déjà occupée par Meta et HTC, une arrivée tardive, un prix au-dessus de tout le monde, un discours sur la manière dont les autres s’y prenaient mal, et une promesse de faire sortir le produit de sa niche. On connaît la suite : environ 390 000 casques écoulés en 2024 selon IDC, 45 000 au dernier trimestre 2025, une chaîne d’assemblage arrêtée dès le début 2025, et un successeur que John Ternus aurait enterré cet été selon Ming-Chi Kuo, Mark Gurman se montrant un peu moins catégorique. L’iPhone Air a rejoint la liste dans la foulée, avec une production réduite un mois après sa sortie et un Air 2 retiré du calendrier. Deux paris de forme, deux déceptions, et voilà un troisième pari de forme, plus cher que les deux premiers.
Sauf que le Vision Pro a échoué pour une raison que son prix a masquée : il ne remplaçait rien. Personne n’a de casque à renouveler. Il fallait convaincre quelqu’un d’acheter un objet de 600 grammes qu’il n’avait jamais possédé, pour des usages qu’il ne pratiquait pas, en plus de tous ses autres appareils, dans une catégorie où Meta avait déjà mis dix ans et des milliards à ne toucher que des joueurs. L’Air a échoué pour la raison inverse : il remplaçait bien un iPhone, mais demandait presque le prix d’un Pro pour perdre un capteur et de l’autonomie, en échange d’une finesse que personne n’avait réclamée. Un compromis sans contrepartie. Le Duo demande aussi de renoncer, à la photo surtout, mais il donne en échange quelque chose que rien d’autre dans la gamme ne donne, 7,6 pouces dans une poche. La finesse était un argument de vitrine, le grand écran est un argument d’usage.
Et surtout, le Duo est un iPhone. Il entre dans le cycle de renouvellement le plus rodé de l’industrie, avec la reprise de l’ancien modèle, le financement à 0 % sur 24 mois, les opérateurs, les accessoires MagSafe dès le premier jour et la migration en dix minutes, dans une catégorie que Samsung alimente depuis huit générations. Apple n’a jamais démocratisé une catégorie au sens de la rendre moins chère, ni l’iPod, ni l’iPhone, ni la Watch. Elle l’a rendue désirable pour des gens qui ne se sentaient pas concernés, puis les volumes ont suivi. Le Vision Pro a raté cette étape parce qu’un casque ne se porte pas en public. Le bon parallèle, si on en veut un, n’est pas le casque, c’est l’Apple Watch de 2015 : plus chère que les concurrentes, incomplète, sans raison d’être évidente, annoncée morte, et qui a fini par se vendre plus que l’horlogerie suisse. Le Duo a une chose que la Watch n’avait pas, un usage clair dès le premier jour. Et une chose qu’elle n’avait pas non plus, un prix qui exclut la plupart des acheteurs d’iPhone.
Le pliant, dernier argument de l’écran
Il y a un deuxième débat, plus glissant, et il est en train de se retourner. Depuis deux ans, on nous explique que l’avenir du smartphone est dans sa disparition : des lunettes avec un agent IA, des écouteurs qui répondent, un assistant capable de fabriquer une application à la volée pour une tâche donnée, plus de rectangle de verre dans la poche.
Sam Altman et Jony Ive travaillent dessus, Meta vend des Ray-Ban par millions, et chaque keynote de constructeur commence désormais par un modèle de langage. Sauf que le premier objet de cette génération, l’AI Pin de Humane, a été débranché au bout d’un an. Le Rabbit R1 a fini dans les tiroirs. Les lunettes Meta se vendent, mais comme accessoire d’un smartphone, et non comme un remplaçant. Apple, qui a passé vingt minutes sur Siri AI ce mercredi 9 septembre, a ensuite passé une heure sur des écrans.
    Pour aller plus loin
            On pensait avoir touché le fond avec le Rabbit R1 et l’Humane Pin, mais l’industrie tech est pleine de ressources
            
C’est là que le Duo m’intéresse plus que ses caméras. Le Duo ne se replie pas pour se faire discret. Il s’ouvre pour offrir plus de surface, plus de fenêtres, plus de contexte à l’IA dont Apple fait la promotion.
Counterpoint le formule : les grands écrans deviennent plus importants « à mesure que les assistants IA passent au multitâche et à l’exécution de tâches sur plusieurs apps ». Autrement dit, le pliant est la réponse du smartphone à ceux qui annoncent sa mort. Plutôt que de disparaître derrière une voix, il double sa dalle et propose d’être l’endroit où l’on voit ce que l’agent fait. On reste dans le super smartphone, loin de l’ère post-smartphone.
On a d’ailleurs listé sept sacrifices en première génération qui rappellent que ce super smartphone n’est pas encore fini.
    Pour aller plus loin
            iPhone Duo : les 7 sacrifices d’Apple, et ce que la version 2 devrait corriger
            
Alors, Apple va-t-elle sauver le pliant ou le tuer ? Ni l’un ni l’autre, à mon avis, et c’est ce qui rend le moment intéressant. Elle va le sortir de l’anonymat sans le sortir de la niche, faire de 2 % du marché un segment qui compte parce qu’il aura son logo dessus, et laisser les constructeurs chinois se battre sur les prix en dessous. Samsung, qui a le même format deux mois plus tôt et 340 euros moins cher, va découvrir ce que ça fait d’avoir eu raison trop tôt. Apple vient de dire, avec deux écrans et une charnière appariée à l’unité en usine, qu’elle ne croit pas à la fin du rectangle. Sept ans après Samsung, Apple ne vient pas légitimer le pliant. Elle légitime l’écran.

            iPhone Duo vs Galaxy Z Fold 8 : l’énorme duel des pliants passeport, poste par poste

articles.title: IBM is launching a new open source AI model to get NASA back to the Moon — and making petabytes of lunar data available to study
articles.text:
IBM is launching a new open source AI model to get NASA back to the Moon — and making petabytes of lunar data available to study
IBM will help NASA researchers analyze decades of lunar observation data
- IBM and NASA launch open source AI model to help further lunar research
- Researchers will be able to better analyze petabytes of Moon data from last five decades
- IBM and NASA also release dataset for public usage and analysis
IBM has launched a new open source AI model it hopes will help spur on NASA researchers in their push to get humanity back to the Moon.
The new NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation model, available on Hugging Face, will allow researchers to analyze decades of lunar observation data, and identify geological features that are critical to understand for NASA as it looks to build a sustained human presence on the Moon.
The model has been trained by IBM and NASA researchers on a huge, multimodal NASA dataset, which will also be released alongside the model, providing wider access to the latest advanced AI systems in a bid to push on wider progress in lunar exploration.
To the Moon (and beyond)
At its most obvious level, the model will allow a much easier way for researchers to study petabytes of data gathered on the Moon's surface for potentially hazardous locations such as ice deposits or craters.
Currently, scientists often rely on manual analysis or low-resolution, task-specific AI models, which can be not only computationally demanding, but also often lack the accuracy needed for detailed geographic analysis.
The new release will now mean that instead of needing to build a new AI model for every potential issue, scientists can now adapt a single foundation model to investigate a range of lunar geologic features.
The model has already proved useful, identifying craters and volcanic features far more accurately (see below) and significantly reducing errors in locating potential ice deposits.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
IBM, which has worked with NASA for over five decades, including on the Apollo missions, believes the model could help future astronauts navigate safely and even find essential resources, as well as helping scientists better understand the Moon's geological history.
“Uncovering the mysteries of the Moon requires an ability to learn from an extraordinary volume of scientific data,” said Juan Bernabe-Moreno, Director of IBM Research Europe, UK and Ireland.
“The NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model gives scientists a foundation to explore the Moon at scale, connecting observations across instruments, revealing patterns that are difficult to see in isolation, and providing an open platform the global research community can build on.”
The release of the dataset will mark the first time a unified, publicly-available cache has been made available and ready for machine learning. It brings together over 30 spatially aligned layers from nine instruments across four missions, including tens of thousands of images and maps showing unique geophysical properties of the lunar surface from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) and NASA’s GRAIL mission.
Identifying lunar ice deposits could be particularly vital, as the presence of both water and oxygen will be crucial to establishing a human base on the Moon, and even creating rocket fuel for future Mars missions.
Scanning the Moon's volcanic features, known as Iregular Mare Patches, can allow scientists to better understand the Moon's volcanic history and thermal evolution, as well as helping identify potential sites for landing and other surface operations.
Finally, studying the Moon's craters can offer a wealth of information on its history, including the age of different terrains, their geology, and even the chemical composition of the early lunar interior - as well as again helping to identify safe landing sites without hazards such as steep slopes and boulders.

articles.title: OpenAI's rogue AI agents accessed more websites to communicate than originally believed — defiant LLMs accessed old wikis and abandoned websites to co-ordinate in a bid to dupe assessors
articles.text:
OpenAI's rogue AI agents accessed more websites to communicate than originally believed — defiant LLMs accessed old wikis and abandoned websites to co-ordinate in a bid to dupe assessors
Dozens of websites, apparently.
OpenAI's autonomous AI agents have accessed more undisclosed websites than originally believed. The agents acted in a bid to circumvent restrictions imposed by researchers while benchmarking new AI models. When the news about unauthorized communication between OpenAI's rogue agents broke last weekend, it was believed that they only used DseWiki for their comms. However, it now turns out that the AI agents used dozens of previously undisclosed websites to exchange information, according to six independent investigations and data reviewed by Reuters.
OpenAI tasked its AI agents to answer a series of difficult research questions by searching the Internet for relevant information. The company let them browse the Internet and read websites, but it explicitly prohibited them from posting or modifying online content. Despite this restriction, between May and July the agents discovered unconventional ways to write to old wikis and abandoned websites, where they left information that other agents could subsequently retrieve to help complete their assigned research tasks.
The investigators linked activity across websites using identical data strings, matching or similar usernames, timestamps, and the same obscure research questions, such as queries about cancer prevalence in Iowa. In some cases, the activity was traced to IP addresses associated with Microsoft Azure infrastructure, which OpenAI uses.
So far, the researchers have identified between 18 and 23 potentially affected sites wherein rogue AI agents communicated, though they believe that there were considerably more websites used to exchange information, but they have not found them yet. Andrew Yoon of California nonprofit CivAI identified 18 previously undisclosed sites; Sydney Von Arx's group discovered credible evidence across 23, while software developer and former congressional aide Kenneth Russell DeGraff found related information on at least 10 sites according to the Reuters report.
The affected resources included collaboratively maintained wikis, text-storage services, and link shorteners operated by Vanderbilt University and the University of Toronto. Other websites were essentially abandoned by their owners. The list of these websites included an Advanced Placement Chemistry wiki created by a Massachusetts high-school teacher in 2008, two personal websites run by Polish technology workers, puzzle-oriented wikis, and a roughly two-decade-old site dedicated to text-editing software.
Perhaps the most alarming thing, besides the fact that AI robots can communicate with each other, is that OpenAI did not disclose how many websites were affected or explain why the activity remained undisclosed for months. It does stress that the scale or seriousness of the said misconduct was well below that of the famous Hugging Face breach in July. Meanwhile, the company reportedly said it is developing a framework for reporting model misalignment across training, evaluation, and deployment and said it will share it soon.

articles.title: China’s drone supremacy shows in airlifting bodies and food after Nepal flood disaster
articles.text:
Chinese-made drones are flying out the bodies of flood victims and delivering food to survivors in the aftermath of devastating flash floods on the border of Nepal and China’s Tibetan region.
Nepal’s army has been using four DJI FlyCart 100 drones donated from China to make 10 to 16 aid deliveries each day, according to Reuters. This comes after a partial glacier collapse in the Himalayan mountains unleashed a sudden surge of water, mud, and debris that swept through border crossings, valley communities, and hydropower projects on August 26.
The DJI Flycart 100 Drones come with a 98-foot rope and winch system for picking up and dropping off heavy loads. The website of Chinese drone company DJI describes the drones as being able to carry between 187 and 220 pounds, depending on the battery configuration.
The four Chinese cargo drones being used by the Nepal army are currently hauling about 132 pounds of supplies per trip, Reuters reported. That heavy-lift capability has also allowed the drones to remove human bodies from some flood-stricken areas.
The official death toll in Nepal had risen to 1,369 as of September 9, according to a situation report from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. The Nepal government agency also reported that more than 5,000 people are still missing, including 587 foreign nationals.
The same situation report also mentioned how the drones have helped to distribute 1,591 kilograms of food items across 31 flights. The United Nations is appealing for $20.5 million to help 43,000 people in the aftermath of the flood disaster in Nepal.
Smaller drones have also proven useful in search-and-rescue efforts as Nepal has deployed more than 21,000 police and soldiers to look for survivors. Search teams have occasionally found surviving workers trapped in hydropower tunnels after the floodwaters ripped through both operational hydropower plants and sites under construction.

articles.title: Other World Computing (OWC) Announces Acquisition of OpenDrives
articles.text:
Thursday, September 10th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
Other World Computing (OWC) Announces Acquisition of OpenDrives
Other World Computing (OWC), a trusted leader in high-performance storage, memory, connectivity, software, and accessories that empower creative and business professionals to maximize performance, enhance reliability, and streamline workflows, today announced the acquisition of OpenDrives, a leader in software-defined video and rich media storage management solutions and data services. 
The addition of OpenDrives' solutions expands OWC's award-winning shared storage portfolio reach with the Jellyfish line into enterprise-scale data management, hybrid cloud orchestration, and edge workflows. OpenDrives' Atlas data storage and management platform has been the preferred solution for leading Hollywood studios, post-production houses, and live broadcast networks since 2011, recognized for reliably handling the low-latency, high-throughput performance required for complex, data-intensive creative environments. In April 2026, the new OpenDrives Edge hybrid cloud-edge performance accelerator was announced, providing widely distributed teams working in edge locations "local speed" data access, without the high costs and complexity involved with traditional hybrid cloud workflows. Evolving customer requirements for infrastructure modernization and their need to bridge ever-expanding data silos, while reducing costs, led to the introduction of the Astraeus cloud-native data services platform, which was released in beta mode for early adopters in late 2025 and will have an updated release in 2027.OWC's acquisition of Jellyfish (LumaForge/2021) gave customers a broader range of high-speed shared storage solutions purpose-built for professional video workflows. Today, Jellyfish supports customers from mobile and desktop production through enterprise-class rackmount, all-flash, and petabyte-scale environments.
"OWC and OpenDrives share so much synergy; we couldn't be more excited about this partnership," said Trevor Morgan, CEO, OpenDrives. "By acquiring and integrating OpenDrives' Atlas, Astraeus, and Edge, OWC now offers an end-to-end data ecosystem—from plug-and-play edit bays to global enterprise pipelines handling uncompressed 8K/12K workflows across on-premises, edge, and hybrid cloud, and OpenDrives' loyal customers can leverage OWC's award-winning portfolio for their direct-attached and shared storage solutions, while expanding their archive and backup with even more cost-effective, widely recognized, and popular storage options."
"OWC has always been about removing the barriers between people and their creative work. Bringing OpenDrives into OWC allows us to take that mission further by connecting the high-performance storage and workflow solutions our customers rely on with powerful software-defined data management services, giving customers a more seamless way to capture, create, collaborate, and access their content wherever their work takes them," said Larry O'Connor, Founder and CEO, Other World Computing (OWC). "I'm also excited to welcome OpenDrives' employees to OWC, broadening our team to more than 250 people around the world."
"OpenDrives has a long history of supporting creators, and we are very pleased that OWC shares that same vision and will continue OpenDrives' legacy of providing the best products to creatives solving the hardest problems," said Joel Whitley, Partner, IAG Capital Partners.

articles.title: Marvel's Wolverine is a solid follow-up to Insomniac's Spider-Man
articles.text:
In many ways, Insomniac Games’ work on the Marvel’s Spider-Man series has been rather definitive. Besides being some of the best licensed games ever made, they’ve come to represent a new era for one of the most prolific developers in the business while also even having clear influences on such massive pieces of media as Spider-Man: Brand New Day.
Naturally, then, people were wondering how the storied PlayStation studio would fare with another, decidedly bloodier Marvel character: Wolverine. Now, five years after the official unveiling of Marvel’s Wolverine, we have an answer. While the game doesn’t quite reach the highs of Marvel’s Spider-Man, it’s very much a worthwhile superhero outing in its own right, offering an exceptional take on the Canucklehead that stands among the finest.
The best there is at what he does
Above all else, Marvel’s Wolverine succeeds, as Marvel’s Spider-Man did before it, in nailing its characters. Through Liam McIntyre’s equal parts ferociously intense and remarkably subdued performance, James “Logan” Howlett is an outstanding lead character. From the very first scene, we see him in an incredibly raw and vulnerable state in the jungle before he’s rescued by biologist Nathaniel Essex (Troy Baker), effectively setting the stage for the rest of the game.
This pairing doesn’t prove quite as emotionally charged as the one between Peter and Otto in Marvel’s Spider-Man, but it’s nonetheless a fascinating inverse of Logan’s longtime dynamic with Charles Xavier in Insomniac’s vision of a Marvel universe before the X-Men. What if, instead of the hopeful and empathetic professor, the perennially lost Logan was guided by a more world-weary and morally dubious Englishman? It’s particularly captivating to see their ideological clashes over how to attain their mutually shared goal of protecting mutants — who are currently largely unknown to the public — from the genocidal Dr. Bolivar Trask (Jason Spisak) and his deadly, cybernetically-enhanced Reavers.
But the beating heart of Marvel’s Wolverine actually lies in his relationship with Jean Grey (Krizia Bajos). While her role in the game has led to much consternation from some comic fans, Insomniac nonetheless tells a meaningfully poignant story about second chances through Logan and Jean.
They’re both reluctant to get close; for him, it’s a sense of self-loathing and fear over his unknown past, and for her, it’s her unrelenting efforts to escape her abusive mother and save her found family of fellow hunted mutants. Seeing them slowly bond over the course of the game, and then having that bond tested amid great adversity, proves to be truly affecting, especially in the finale and its implications for potential future games.
Mr. Worldwide
The strength of that relationship and the narrative pacing as a whole are aided immensely by the game’s structure. Where the Marvel’s Spider-Man series lets you swing around an open-world NYC, Marvel’s Wolverine is a tightly-crafted globe-trotting adventure that takes you to the likes of Telembang, Japan, Madripoor and, yes, even Wolverine’s native Canada. (Vancouver is the game’s main Canadian location, and it’s substantial, but Wolverine’s Team X, which is led by Essex and includes Sabretooth, Mystique and fellow Canuck Walter Langkowski, is actually based in Yukon. Kudos to Canadian art director Gavin Goulden and the rest of Insomniac for this wonderful — and all-too rare — opportunity for Canada to play itself.)
Because of Marvel’s Wolverine‘s linearity, Insomniac is able to dedicate significant amounts of time to Logan and his allies working together closely to traverse immaculately detailed areas to the tune of David Fleming’s sublime Western- and Asian-infused score. Nothing endears you to Logan and Jean more than seeing them saunter through the rich neon-soaked streets of Japan’s Kabukicho entertainment district as they bicker like an old married couple.
All the while, it’s refreshing to have a more purposeful, focused experience, especially as other recent action games like Onimusha: Way of the Sword arguably overstay their welcome. I rolled credits after around 15 hours, which is a decent length after having taken my time soaking in the sights, and unlocked the Platinum trophy about seven hours later.
And honestly, that optional content is absolutely worth your while. The biggest of these sidequests, Nightmare Doors, are various challenges scattered throughout each level that centre around traversal and combat. Clearing them will unlock short narrated stories that unravel scenes from Wolverine’s tragic past in sombre and even harrowing ways.
And picking up from Insomniac’s stellar work on Spider-Man, the collectible whisky bottles that you can find for stat-boosting Adaptations all have juicy bits of narrative injected into them, with Logan recalling fond memories he associates with each drink, such as one gifted to him by Essex when he was welcomed into Team X.
All killer, (somewhat) no filler
If you’ve been wondering why I’ve waited this long to talk about the combat, it’s because it is, lamentably, the weakest part of Marvel’s Wolverine. To be clear, it’s by no means bad, with Wolverine’s barrage of claw attacks packing a viscerally satisfying weight as you skewer foes left and right. This cinematic flair is only enhanced by dramatic camera effects that focus on close-ups of Wolverine’s claws piercing enemies, intense feedback from the DualSense controller and McIntyre’s deafening battle cries. What’s more, pressing Triangle to instantly leap towards enemies in range like a pouncing animal is undeniably thrilling, particularly when Wolverine fully tackles wounded foes to the ground to allow you to repeatedly stab them.
Unfortunately, a sense of weary repetition eventually settles in due to the relatively small lack of variety in Wolverine’s moveset. Indeed, there’s a glacial pace at which you unlock new Techniques, including a crowd-controlling flurry attack, screwdriver horizontal launch and a few others, including one surprise I won’t spoil. To Insomniac’s credit, the enemy variety is unexpectedly vast, from basic firearm-equipped Reavers to the frenetic Hand ninjas and even frighteningly resilient Sentinel Bots, as well as hazards like healing-stunting blades and mutant inhibitor generators. But even then, they feel squandered when they’re pretty much all overcome by mashing Square.
Because of this, the otherwise optional stealth just never feels worth pursuing, even with the incredibly cool effect of Wolverine’s primal hunter senses creating a ghastly blue highlight around enemies’ skeletons.
Ironically, the combat really comes alive in the aforementioned late-game Nightmare challenges once you have Wolverine’s full arsenal unlocked. One of them in particular, a series of wave-based gauntlets, throws all kinds of these enemies at you, creating a welcome level of tension. Here, you have to actually balance Wolverine’s tier-based Rage Mode (the third of which paints the world in sumptuous grey-and-black hues while unlocking brutal insta-kills) with its Last Stand ability to expend the full metre to provide a fatally wounded Wolverine with a burst of health.
All of this — accompanied with juggling cooldowns on all of your unlocked special Techniques and their associated invincibility frames, the various kinds of contextual parries, that aforementioned special late-game ability and Adaptations — actually lends a dynamic, balletic rhythm to fights. Here, I found myself actually dying several times because I missed a parry, failed to take out a supernatural Hand threat or didn’t use my Technique that temporarily boosted my healing factor at the right time. It added a layer of depth to the combat that I wish was present beyond the game’s final stretch.
The setpieces in Marvel’s Wolverine are also sadly hit-or-miss. Even removing my Canadian bias, the standout is actually the convoy chase on B.C.’s Sea-to-Sky Highway, with Wolverine zipping along the roads to slash at foes while lovingly rendered Squamish signs pass overhead. But other setpieces, like an escape from an exploding factory with Jean or an assault on an aerial plane, are painfully rigid and, worse still, have several dated slow-motion quick-time events. While I don’t fault these segments for being highly scripted and cinematic, even a bit more freedom to run and jump instead of often just moving in a literal straight line would have gone a long way.
Ain’t no hero
Marvel’s Wolverine is a worthy follow-up to Insomniac’s Marvel’s Spider-Man series. Although the game’s uneven action leaves it unable to fully reach those amazing highs of its predecessors, it tells a genuinely heartfelt story of Wolverine, Jean Grey and this first generation of mutants while teeing up a tantalizing future for them. Only time will tell where Insomniac may next take all of these characters, but after this strong first outing, I, for one, am X-cited to go along for the ride.
Marvel’s Wolverine launches exclusively on PS5 on September 15.

articles.title: 2.300 Euro für ein iPhone Duo? Diese Dinge könntest du stattdessen kaufen
articles.text:
2.300 Euro für ein iPhone Duo? Diese Dinge könntest du stattdessen kaufen
Hinweis: Wir haben in diesem Artikel Provisions-Links verwendet und sie durch "*" gekennzeichnet. Erfolgt über diese Links eine Bestellung, erhält t3n.de eine Provision.
Foldables können praktisch sein. Mit einem Handgriff wird aus einem normalgroßen Smartphone ein kleines Tablet. Weil das technisch aufwendig ist, sind die Geräte allerdings seit jeher sehr teuer. Das beste Beispiel ist das neue iPhone Duo von Apple. Es kommt mit dem aktuell stärksten Prozessor, einem Titangehäuse und einem ausgeklügelten Faltmechanismus – kostet Kund:innen bei Marktstart aber auch mindestens 2.300 Euro.
Für das Geld bekommt man allerdings auch in Zeiten der Speicherkrise einiges an mehr an Technik als „nur“ die Smartphone-Tablet-Kombination. Es folgt eine kleine, keineswegs vollständige Übersicht.
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 – wenn es faltbar bleiben soll
Dass das iPhone Duo in den kommenden Wochen und Monaten signifikant günstiger werden wird, kann man so gut wie ausschließen. Obwohl sich Foldables noch in einer Nische bewegen, sagten Analyst:innen schon lange vorab voraus, dass sich das Duo millionenfach verkaufen wird. Wenn das eintritt, gibt es für Apple und Händler keinen Grund, die Preise zu senken. Anders sieht das bei Samsung aus.
Das Galaxy Z Fold 8 bietet zwar weniger durchdachte Software-Funktionen und Design-Elemente, kommt aber im selben Format wie das iPhone Duo und ist anders als Apple-Geräte weniger wertstabil. Ursprünglich begann die Preisspanne bei 1.999 Euro. Selbst damit hätte ihr 300 Euro gespart. Mittlerweile gibt es das Fold 8 aber etablierten Händlern wie Notebooksbilliger* schon für 1.449 Euro. Auf den etablierten Vergleichsplattformen finden sich zudem Ebay- und kleinere Händler, die den Preis bereits weiter reduziert haben. Ihr spart also mindestens 950 Euro.
Das ist ausreichend Budget, um zusätzlich noch ein neues Macbook zu kaufen. Für ein Macbook Neo reicht das Geld locker. Ebenfalls bei Notebooksbilliger* und bei Cyberport gibt es den Apple-Laptop bereits ab 669 Euro. Die teurere Variante mit 512 Gigabyte Speicher und Touch-ID-Sensor bekommt ihr bei NBB* , Cyberport* und Otto für rund 770 Euro. Und es bleiben weitere 250 Euro übrig.
Die Apple-Vollausstattung
Statt ein einziges iPhone zu kaufen, bekommt ihr für 2.300 Euro problemlos auch die Apple-Vollausstattung aus iPhone, iPad und Apple Watch. Dazu müsst ihr nicht einmal auf ältere Modelle zurückgreifen. Das neue iPhone 18 Pro kostet zwar 1.449 Euro, da bleibt aber noch Spielraum. Die neue Apple Watch Series 12 kostet euch 449 Euro mit kleinem und 499 Euro mit großem Bildschirm. Ein iPad 10 lässt sich dann noch mit Glück für 400 Euro abstauben.
Die Android-Vollausstattung
Setzt ihr stattdessen auf Android, habt ihr noch bessere Chancen, günstig davon zu kommen. Amazon* bietet das neue Pixel 11 Pro mit KI-Fokus zum Beispiel schon für rund 1.070 statt 1.199 Euro an. Wie beim Galaxy Z Fold 8 gilt: Kleinere Shops und Ebay können den Preis sogar noch unterbieten. Ebenfalls bei Amazon* bekommt ihr die Pixel Watch 5 ab 419 Euro. Da bleiben mehr als 800 Euro für ein zusätzliches Tablet wie das Samsung Galaxy Tab S11, das ihr für Preise zwischen 670 und 700 Euro bekommt. Und wieder bleibt noch etwas Geld übrig.
Ein starker Mac
Auch, wenn Apple die Preise für seine Macs mittlerweile angezogen hat: Für 2.300 Euro kann man da schon einiges bekommen – zum Beispiel den neuen Mac Mini mit M6-Prozessor, 32 Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher und ein Terabyte großer SSD. Damit sollte der kleine Computer gut genug ausgestattet sein, um viele lokale KI-Modelle händeln zu können oder aber als Zwischenstation für Openclaw zu dienen. Es bleiben sogar noch 260 Euro vom Budget übrig.
Ein starkes Macbook
Soll es portabel sein? Dann gibt es auch hier bei Apple selbst viel Power. Etwa ein Macbook Air mit 15-Zoll-Bildschirm, 24 Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher und ein Terabyte großer SSD. Bei Cyberport* bekommt ihr diese Konfiguration aktuell sogar für rund 2.040 Euro. Bei einem Macbook Pro sieht es dagegen nicht ganz so gut. Das Budget reicht nur für die Grundversion mit M5-Chip, 16 Gigabyte und 512 Gigabyte.

articles.title: Gemini por fin lanza su app de escritorio para Windows, con Gemini Spark y Omni integrados
articles.text:
Meses después de su lanzamiento en macOS, Gemini por fin estrena su app de escritorio para Windows. De esta manera, la IA de Google ahora dispone de un cliente nativo para el software de Microsoft y abre la puerta a un uso más integrado en cualquier PC, sin depender de un navegador web ni del móvil.
Uno de los puntos más atractivos de la app de Gemini para Windows es que integra dos de las mejores herramientas de la firma californiana. Nos referimos puntualmente a Gemini Spark y a Omni, que se encuentran entre las soluciones más potentes que brindan los de Mountain View en la actualidad.
Quienes instalen la app de Gemini en su PC con Windows podrán invocar a Gemini Spark para que realice tareas de forma automatizada, incluso aunque involucren varios pasos complejos. Es importante recordar que esta herramienta vendría a ser el equivalente de OpenClaw desarrollado por Google.
En el caso de Omni, la herramienta permite crear fotos y vídeos realistas directamente desde la interfaz del cliente nativo de Gemini. Entre tantas funciones, destaca la opción de extender un vídeo ya existente por hasta 40 segundos en lotes con una duración máxima de 10 segundos cada uno.
La app de Gemini para Windows ya se puede instalar de forma gratuita
Por supuesto que el uso principal de Gemini a través de la app de escritorio está destinado al chatbot homónimo. Al igual que con el cliente para Mac, la versión para Windows permite invocar al chatbot usando un atajo de teclado. En los PC con el sistema operativo de Microsoft, el acceso rápido a la IA de Google se activa pulsando Alt + Barra espaciadora.
La aplicación de Gemini para Windows se puede descargar de forma gratuita desde este enlace. El acceso a Gemini Spark requiere de una suscripción de pago a Google AI y su acceso está restringido a mayores de 18 años.
La disponibilidad de esta característica puede estar limitada regionalmente, aunque el resto de las funciones de Gemini están habilitadas en una gran cantidad de países. Si en el tuyo ya se puede usar Gemini desde la web o el móvil, también puedes acceder a los clientes de escritorio.
Los requisitos para instalar Gemini son mínimos, puesto que la aplicación es compatible tanto con Windows 10 como con Windows 11. Además, ofrece instaladores tanto para procesadores x86, como los de Intel o AMD, como para los ordenadores con chips basados en ARM, como los Snapdragon X de Qualcomm o el RTX Spark de NVIDIA.

articles.title: Proxima Fusion bets €140M on a critical fusion ingredient dominated by Asian suppliers | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Proxima Fusion is betting on a critical ingredient for its fusion reactors: superconducting tape.
Proxima Fusion said Wednesday it plans to build a €140 million ($162.6 million) factory to produce fusion-grade high-temperature superconducting (HTS) tape, which will provide the startup with key component to its reactor design.
The move comes months after Proxima raised €411 million in a round that catapulted the company up the ranks of the best-funded fusion startups. The Germany-based fusion startup plans to use a mix of public and private funding to complete the factory, with the state of Lower Saxony chipping in €21 million.
Proxima will use HTS tape to generate powerful magnetic fields to contain the plasma required to spark fusion reactions.
The startup’s demonstration plant will use 20,000 kilometers of HTS tape, while its commercial power plant will need twice as much. Today, the vast majority of HTS tape is made in China and Japan.
HTS tape emerged a little over a decade ago as one of the fundamental breakthroughs that enabled the current generation of fusion power startups. Because it can generate strong magnetic fields at relatively high temperatures, HTS tape enables smaller and more efficient reactor designs.
While fusion power is expected to consume a large portion of the world’s HTS tape production, other companies like Veir are using it to boost the efficiency and power density of data centers.

articles.title: Six Hours on the Runway: Lessons in AI and Air Traffic Control- EE Times
articles.text:
In the engineering world, we are taught at college or university to think about worst-case scenarios and plan for them to ensure systems are resilient. But this week, while sitting on a plane for six hours on the runway at Heathrow Airport amid a total shutdown of the airport caused by a flight-processing system glitch in the U.K.’s national air traffic control system, operated by a body called National Air Traffic Services (NATS), I naturally started to wonder what backup systems might have been in place to avoid such massive disruption.
To set the scene, I was on a flight scheduled to depart at 12:50 p.m. for New York’s JFK Airport. I had boarded around 11:45 a.m. and was sitting in my exit row seat with legroom for the six-hour flight when the pilot announced around 12:48 p.m. that no flights were taking off because of a radar control problem.
The reason wasn’t a problem with the aircraft. It wasn’t the weather. It wasn’t a shortage of pilots or a strike. Nor was it, as in the case of a cancelled flight I was supposed to take to Dallas Fort Worth back in May this year, a problem with automatic cabin pressurization motors failing. As it transpired from an official statement from NATS on Tuesday (Sept. 8) at 3:25 p.m., the issue was in its flight processing system. I was constantly following the situation on my plane’s onboard fast Starlink Wi-Fi, and when I saw the statement at 4:40 p.m. saying that they’d found a fix, I was hopeful that we’d take off for New York.
Alas, no. By 6:35 p.m., the airline told us it was still not able to take off, and that the flight would be cancelled. So, no New York for me this week.
Resilience is not just about building in redundancy
The NATS statement suggests the problem was within its systems, since airspace itself remained open. The failure of a key element—the software—in the infrastructure had effectively immobilized aircraft, crew, and passengers and created knock-on disruption across an entire aviation network. Press reports suggest that airlines were still dealing with displaced aircraft and crews, while cancellations had risen to more than 1,750 flights. I was just one tiny part of this statistic.
I looked for any history of failures in the NATS systems and found details of a previous U.K. air traffic control failure on Aug. 28, 2023. There is nothing about this week’s incident that suggests it was the same type of failure, but it’s worth considering in terms of technological resilience—a theme cited extensively in the detailed report into what went wrong in the air traffic control system in that accident.
In the August 2023 disruption, NATS’s flight plan reception suite automated (FPRSA-R) software system received a transatlantic flight plan containing a highly unusual combination of six attributes. That combination created an exception the software could not process. The system responded by doing what it was designed to do when it could not guarantee the integrity of the information: It stopped automatic processing rather than risk sending inaccurate flight information to controllers. The problem was compounded because the backup system encountered the same condition.
Although NATS had redundancy, the primary and backup systems were exposed to the same underlying software logic. This forced flight plans to be entered manually, and the slower manual processing meant NATS had to impose severe restrictions on U.K. airspace. The system failed in a way intended to protect safety; the consequence was a massive loss of capacity.
The investigation found that the system contained NATS’s intended logic for dealing with this situation, but one part of that logic had inadvertently not been incorporated into the manufacturer’s FPRSA-R software: The particular combination of six flight-plan attributes was considered so unusual that it wasn’t included in the formal test program. The report explicitly acknowledged that it is impossible to foresee and test every possible combination of interacting attributes.
An independent review by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) produced multiple recommendations, most of which were implemented by NATS. One of these was to review its policy on software diversity and to understand which systems have diversity and which do not.
If anything was learned from that 2023 incident, it’s that building in redundancy alone is not resilience. You can have a primary system and a backup system, but if both depend on the same software logic, the same data, the same assumptions, or the same operational processes, they can fail together. The response to the 2023 incident recognized this.
The 2023 incident indicated that a highly complex, safety-critical, centrally interconnected software system can fail catastrophically when it encounters a data combination that was not anticipated, even when the individual components and their conventional backups are functioning correctly.
Can we upgrade systems or use AI to avoid such failures?
In this current era of AI hype, I did wonder what role AI has here or whether aviation infrastructure could be smarter. After all, we are living through an extraordinary period of technological optimism. AI can write software, generate designs, optimize logistics, predict failures, and increasingly make decisions autonomously. But none of that automatically makes the infrastructure on which our physical world depends more resilient.
We also talk about smarter systems. But the harder problem isn’t always making a system smarter. Sometimes, it is making sure that a system that was built decades ago can continue operating safely when something unexpected happens.
In safety-critical infrastructure, we can’t ‘just replace it with something newer’. A modern cloud-native architecture might be much more flexible. AI could potentially help with anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, traffic optimization, and recovery. But aviation systems have a safety case that cannot just be modified because new AI-enabled software is available. Any change potentially has to demonstrate that the new system is at least as safe as the old one.
It’s not that engineering cannot rise to the challenge. It’s more about the old system being a known quantity, which has been tested against enormous numbers of operational scenarios. Its failure modes are understood. Regulators have certified it. Controllers have learned how to work with it. Airlines, airports, and adjacent systems have interfaces built around it.
The irony is that the very characteristics that make a safety-critical system trustworthy can also make it extremely difficult to modernize.
And this is where AI could help: not to replace the legacy system, but to help understand, monitor, and gradually modernize the system without losing the safety properties that took decades to establish.
The legacy systems may not be ready for AI in the control loop, but AI could help with tasks such as:
- identifying anomalous data patterns before they trigger a failure;
- analyzing huge volumes of system logs;
- identifying interactions between components that humans haven’t anticipated;
- testing millions of unusual combinations in simulation;
- generating synthetic edge cases;
- predicting where ageing infrastructure is becoming fragile;
- assisting engineers in understanding undocumented legacy code.
What did I learn from being stuck on the aircraft for six hours going nowhere? Legacy technologies in industries such as aviation can be highly sophisticated but extraordinarily difficult to change. The challenge for engineers developing next-generation technologies isn’t simply to make systems smarter. It is to make them capable of anticipating the unexpected, recovering gracefully, and continuing to operate when the technology around them doesn’t.

articles.title: Swish raises $24M led by Bertelsmann India
articles.text:
Swish raises $24M led by Bertelsmann India
The quick-service food delivery platform will use the funds to expand its kitchen network and supply chain infrastructure to meet growing demand.
Quick-service food delivery platform Swish has raised $24 million in a funding round led by Bertelsmann India Investments, with participation from existing investors Accel, Bain Capital Ventures, and Hara Global.
Swish will use the funds to expand its kitchen network and supply chain infrastructure to meet growing demand. Founded in 2024 by Aniket Shah, Ujjwal Sukheja, and Saran S, the startup currently serves Bengaluru, Gurugram, Noida, Delhi and Ghaziabad.
Swish is building a vertically integrated, high-density network of neighbourhood kitchens that cook fresh food and deliver it within an average radius of one kilometre. By controlling the kitchen, technology and delivery experience end-to-end, Swish aims to optimise simultaneously for speed, quality and price.
According to the company, since March this year, its monthly orders have tripled and it now serves over a million orders a month. The startup says its neighbourhood kitchens model can turn around thousands of orders a day with an average preparation time of under four minutes.
The menu on the platform has grown to more than 250 SKUs across 20+ food categories. Lunch and dinner have overtaken snacks, while late-night cravings are one of the key demand drivers, said the company.
"The food services market is about $100B in size, with online food delivery still capturing less than 10% of the market today. An average Indian consumer consumes food 90–100 times a month, but orders online only 4 times out of it. Getting fresh, delicious food at the best prices in 10 minutes is an incredibly delightful experience, and our ambition is to make this possible for 100 million consumers and capture a large share of this $100B opportunity,” said Aniket Shah, Co-founder and CEO, Swish.
Pankaj Makkar, Managing Director, Bertelsmann India Investments, said, “Everyday food is the biggest under-served category in Indian consumption, and it has remained that way because no one has managed freshness, affordability and convenience at the same time. Aniket, Ujjwal, Saran and team have built the kitchens, the logistics and the technology to do exactly that. It is once again a category defining investment from our side."
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: iPhone Duo : Apple a pris une décision radicale pour gonfler l'autonomie
articles.text:
Surprise, alors que la majorité des téléphones pliants présentent un tiroir SIM physique, Apple a pris une décision radicale en n’en intégrant pas à son iPhone Duo. Autrement dit, l’iPhone pliant est uniquement eSIM. Cette caractéristique n’est pas limitée à un marché : tous les iPhone Duo commercialisés dans le monde seront uniquement eSIM.
L’iPhone pliant est uniquement eSIM
Apple vient tout juste de dévoiler son premier pliant : l’iPhone Duo, soit son iPhone le plus cher jamais commercialisé. Parmi toutes ses caractéristiques dévoilées, nous avons pu apprendre que ce téléphone n’intègre pas de tiroir SIM physique. Autrement dit, il est uniquement eSIM. Inutile donc d’espérer placer votre carte SIM physique dans le téléphone, cela sera tout simplement impossible. À noter que cette caractéristique ne sera pas limitée à un marché : tous les iPhone Duo commercialisés dans le monde seront uniquement eSIM. Ceux qui achèteront un iPhone Duo devront donc convertir leur carte SIM physique en eSIM auprès de leur opérateur.
Apple fait un choix assez radical, là où Samsung a intégré à son Galaxy Z Fold8 un tiroir pour carte SIM physique, tout en proposant également l’eSIM. De façon plus générale, les téléphones pliants des concurrents d’Apple présentent un tiroir SIM. L’iPhone Duo se distingue donc particulièrement sur ce point précis.
Pourquoi l’iPhone Duo est uniquement eSIM ?
Apple a décidé de ne pas intégrer de tiroir SIM dans l’iPhone Duo tout simplement pour libérer de l’espace à l’intérieur du téléphone. La firme de Cupertino a ainsi pu placer une batterie plus importante, ainsi que les différents composants du téléphone, sans être limitée par un espace dédié aux cartes SIM. Pour rappel, le téléphone intègre deux batteries, une dans chaque moitié de l’appareil. L’intégration d’un tiroir SIM physique aurait créé un déséquilibre entre les deux parties du téléphone.
Au passage, cela permet à Apple de proposer un téléphone particulièrement fin. Pour rappel, l’iPhone Air n’intègre pas de tiroir SIM. Les raisons sont quasiment les mêmes : libérer de l’espace pour permettre d’intégrer des pièces importantes, comme la batterie, et rendre le téléphone particulièrement fin. À terme, le tiroir SIM risque de disparaître de façon générale. Si l’iPhone 18 Pro et l’iPhone 18 Pro Max en intègrent toujours un, cela ne risque pas d’être le cas pour les générations futures.
